result:
Solution 1 is correct under the literal reading of the conditions. I derived the p = 2 cases myself, but I did not independently verify the odd-prime case (only p = 3 was considered, not all odd p), so the answer 24 rests partly on trusting the claim that no odd prime works.

**p = 2.** Here f(x) = x⁴ − 4xᵐ − 4xⁿ − 1 with n ∈ {1, 3} and m ∈ {1, 2, 3} \ {n}. I checked each pair:
- (m, n) = (2, 1): f(−1) = 1 − 4 + 4 − 1 = 0, so it is reducible.
- (m, n) = (3, 1): f(i) = 1 + 4i − 4i − 1 = 0, so x² + 1 divides f and it is reducible.
- (m, n) = (1, 3): this is the same polynomial as (3, 1), so it is reducible.
- (m, n) = (2, 3): f(−1) = 1 − 4 + 4 − 1 = 0. Expanding (x+1)(x³ − 5x² + x − 1) gives x⁴ − 4x³ − 4x² − 1, so it is reducible.

All four triples (2,2,1), (2,3,1), (2,1,3), (2,2,3) are admissible. Their sums are 5 + 6 + 6 + 7 = 24.

**Odd p.** Solution 1's reduction mod p and valuation argument at x = ±1 is sound. It forces any factorization to have two factors of degree p, congruent to xᵖ + 1 and xᵖ − 1 mod p. Solution 1 then claims by exhaustive matching that p = 3 gives nothing; I did not re-run that check.

**Solution 2** drops the triples with m < n, namely (2,1,3) and (2,2,3). The problem only requires m ≠ n, both below 2p, so these are admissible. Its answer 11 is wrong.

**Solution 3** wrongly claims (2,2,3) is irreducible, when f(−1) = 0 shows it is reducible. Its answer 17 is wrong.

VERDICT 1: ACCEPT
VERDICT 2: REJECT
VERDICT 3: REJECT
